speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: REPORT ON PROPOSED FLOODING OF SKAGIT RIVER VALLEY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table the International Joint Commission's report on the environmental and ecological consequences in Canada of raising Ross Lake in the Skagit Valley on the west coast.
As hon. members know, the International Joint Commission was asked earlier this year to study a proposal to flood the Upper Skagit Valley in British Columbia. The commission's report, which I have just tabled, has been submitted to the governments of Canada and the United States in response to a request from Ottawa and Washington to review the environmental consequences of raising the Ross dam in the state of Washington on the other side of the border. I would like to thank the six-member International Joint Commission for preparing its report on such short notice. Since April, 1971, it has held hearings on the west coast and carried out various studies, the results of which are being made public in our two national capitals today.
The commissioners report that the High Ross reservoir, were it to be filled, would flood 10 of the 15 miles of the reach of the Skagit River that is the most suitable for fishing and recreational pursuits. It would inundate approximately 5,180 acres in Canada. This is more than 40 per cent of the 10,550 acres of reasonably flat land in the valley.
The commission finds that the Skagit Valley is an uncommon and non-restorable area and has important social values. It also finds that this flooding will result in the loss, in varying degrees, of some important elements of the local environment and, to use its own words, a simplification of the ecology. The commission also tells us that:
The time limitations of this study precluded obtaining information on the cost of mitigating the effects of flooding in the valley.
The quotation continues:
In the absence of knowledge of the costs of protection and enhancement and having only rough estimates of the benefits that might accrue, the commission recommends that these mitigative measures be fully studied before the Ross dam is raised, and that they be undertaken to the extent that the government agencies concerned find them feasible.
Finally, the International Joint Commission tells us that:
Under normal conditions, a study of environmental and ecological conditions should encompass three full years. In contrast, this study was conducted over a period of four months, from early June when public hearings were held, to early October. Therefore, the investigation of the advisory group consisted mainly of an interpretation of raw, and sometimes incomplete, data collected by others and to a review of published reports.
The Canadian government's position is that these environmental and ecological conditions should be fully understood and carefully assessed before any additional flooding is contemplated in the Upper Skagit Valley in British Columbia.
We shall, of course, be examining the International Joint Commission's report in detail, as will the government of British Columbia and the relevant authorities in the United States. After we have completed this review, we will again be discussing the future of the Skagit Valley with our opposite numbers in Victoria and Washington, D.C. The government will be making a further report to the House at that time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REPORT ON PROPOSED FLOODING OF SKAGIT RIVER VALLEY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the excerpts from the International Joint Commission's report quoted by the minister confirm the impression widely held in British Columbia, which I share, that the Skagit Valley is an uncommon and nonrestorable area which has important social values. It also finds that flooding will result in the loss in varying degrees of some important elements of the local environment and a simplification of the ecology. In other words, the study confirms the impressions generally held in that region concerning the importance of preserving the environment in the Skagit Valley and the damage that would be done by flooding.
My impression from the brief excerpts the minister has read from the IJC report is that the commission did not consider banning or recommending indefinite postponement of the actual flooding. The commission did not consider recommending the deferment of the hydroelectric development. The commission's recommendations seem to be confined to the scope of measures which might be taken to mitigate the damage that would be done to the environment in the Skagit Valley. As I say, this is the impression one gets from the excerpts given us by the minister. It is disappointing to many, including myself, that the International Joint Commission did not recommend abandonment of the flooding and seems to confine its recommendations simply to mitigating the damages that might be caused by such flooding. However, the commission has emphasized the importance of preserving the valley. It has emphasized that the damage which it predicts would be done would be irreparable.

In these circumstances I think it is urgent that the minister and the government act with great vigour. When the minister speaks about studying the report and then taking action, quite frankly this does not suggest very much to me in the way of vigour. I would have thought the minister would promptly study the report and would have come before the House with a definite recommendation on how he and the government intend to proceed. It is necessary to act with vigour to preserve a valley that the International Joint Commission has recognized as important, a valley that it has recognized as being threatened. I hope, therefore, that the minister will in fact act with more vigour than his statement to the House this morning seems to indicate. Indeed, now that the Prime Minister has demonstrated that he has great success with President Nixon and he has been able to make breakthroughs there and to persuade the President to give fantastic assurances to Canada, perhaps the minister may be able to persuade the Prime Minister to take up the case directly with the President.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON PROPOSED FLOODING OF SKAGIT RIVER VALLEY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of the Skagit Valley has been before the House for almost two years now and today the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) has presented us with a very attractively wrapped Christmas present. Our problem is that we like the wrapping but we are not certain at the moment what is inside. We hope that some time we can open it up and perhaps even ventilate the whole issue. That would be nice.
The statement of the minister seems to be hopeful. The government seems to be saying rather piously that at the moment the flooding should not be proceeded with. The statement also seems to confirm what the people of British Columbia have felt for some time, that since this valley is one of the last remaining unspoiled recreational resources adjacent to a large population centre it should not be flooded.
Unfortunately, when the agreement of 1942 was reached and the decision to go ahead was made, environmental and recreational matters were not of the consequence that they are today. There was not general public appreciation of the value of this kind of unspoiled resource. The International Joint Commission because of the terms of reference given to it on April 7, 1971, could hardly reverse its position of 1942 even though it may have genuinely felt that the earlier decision was in error. The commission was locked in by government terms of reference so narrow that all it could comment on was the extent of the environmental consequences. I felt last April that this was a delaying tactic and that ultimately the axe would fall on the Skagit Valley and we were just going to be let down easily. I suppose today I am still suspicious or at least fearful that the flooding will occur eventually. I hope we can have an end to or at least an amelioration of the environmental irritants-that seems to be a popular word lately-in Canada-U.S. relations. There have been several environmental irritants lately, as well as economic ones, involving such things as nuclear blasts, oil tankers and the Skagit Valley.
I think it is important that the government indicate frankly what it is going to do. The minister's statement

seems to say that more time is required to study this matter, that the government is going to wind it down, and diffuse the issue. It will not satisfy the people of British Columbia to learn before too long that the minister has allowed the flooding to be proceeded with. What BC citizens want to know is What the government is going to do to stop it. That is really the only solution that will be acceptable in British Columbia.
Perhaps the minister, as he hints in the last paragraph of the statement, might be encouraged to open up bilateral talks with the United States in the hope that the people in Washington, who are also aware of the public concern for environmental matters these days, will realize it is sheer lunacy to continue to flood recreational areas near large urban centres. This will be in keeping with the sentiment in Canada that as Canadians we are no longer content to be hewers of wood and storers of water.

subsubtopic: REPORT ON PROPOSED FLOODING OF SKAGIT RIVER VALLEY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I received at the very last minute the text of the report the minister has just tabled, and in English only. However, I shall not deprive myself of my right to congratulate the International Joint Commission on its study and on the report it has submitted.
We are glad the hon. minister has, according to his statement, committed himself to follow closely the consequences of construction of the dam and, if possible, to prevent it in order not to deprive the people of Canada again of their environment, their heritage and to ensure a sound environment for the future.

The House resumed, from Thursday, December 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benson for the third reading of Bill C-259, to amend the Income Tax Act and to make certain provisions and alterations in the statute law related to or consequential upon the amendments to that
Income Tax Act
act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McCleave (P. 10547).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is not able to be present. I understand this is not possible in view of the meetings with Prime Minister Heath. I wish he were present because I would rather say some of the things I am going to say in his presence than in his absence. I think I should begin by thanking the Prime Minister for his graciousness in delivering his speech to the House of Commons yesterday.
Hear, hear!

I was looking forward to the experience with great pleasure, since the Prime Minister speaks to us so rarely. But I was disappointed because I expected the right hon. gentleman to do better than read some excerpts from old speeches by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), with a little prologue on heavy water which seemed to have been written by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay). The Prime Minister dilated considerably on the length of time the tax reform process had taken and said the only thing that dragged on so slowly in the country in recent years was the heavy water plant at Glace Bay. Obviously, Sir, the goal of attaining a just society has disappeared completely from the Prime Minister's mind. I, too, regret the time and cost involved in the heavy water plant, but I regret particularly that the Prime Minister of Canada has added years of time and tens of millions of dollars to the cost of completing that plant by refusing, for purely partisan reasons, to enter into an arrangement with a Conservative premier of Nova Scotia similar to the arrangement he has now made with the Liberal premier of Nova Scotia.
Hear, hear!

Indeed, in order to find a comparably narrow, partisan behaviour on the part of a Canadian Prime Minister I think one would have to go back at least as far as Mackenzie King's famous "not one five-cent" speech. I regret, too, the length of time the tax reform process has taken. Not only do I regret the length of time, but also the completely inexcusable result of that process which we are now discussing. Both this monstrous bill and the behaviour of the government leading up to the presentation to this House of Bill C-259 are inexcusable.
Back in the fall of 1967 when I first entered this House I asked the then Minister of Finance, the now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), when we were going to receive the white paper on tax reform arising out of the report of the Carter Commission. He said a white paper would be presented near the beginning of 1968. He later made the same kind of statement to the then leader of the NDP in the House that this white paper would be presented as nearly as possible to the commencement of 1968. But, of course, nothing happened.
Then we had a change of ministers of finance, and instead of the white paper on tax reform we had what you

December 17, 1971
Income Tax Act
might call a mini tax reform package from the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) involving in particular consideration of estate and gift taxation. The Minister of Finance started this process late in 1968 when he overhauled and greatly increased the gift and estate taxes. The proposals were made in the mini-budget in the fall of 1968. There was a tremendous row in the country, a tremendous unsettlement, particularly among the backbenchers of the Liberal party, and following the Christmas recess, during which Liberal backbenchers consulted with their constituents, the minister modified his proposals to some degree. Nevertheless, he pushed through complex and rigid gift and estate tax changes, and obviously he put these forward very earnestly as an important reform in the permanent tax laws of this country.
Bear in mind that these changes came about 18 months after the previous minister of finance had promised a white paper on tax reform, and they came less than a year prior to the white paper of the present Minister of Finance. These changes in gift and estate taxes were put forward and fought for very earnestly by the minister as very significant changes in the tax laws of this country. Now, some two years later, the same minister introduces a bill repealing all federal gift and estate taxes, doing away with all of what he put before the House two years previously and all that he had fought for in the House. In other words, all the trouble to which the Minister of Finance put the House and the country with his gift and estate tax changes early in 1969 were a complete waste of the time of the House and of the time of the country.
Hear, hear!

Yet, on the other side of the House they talk about the opposition wasting the time of the House. There you have a so-called mini tax reform which was completely abolished within two years-a complete waste of time. The Minister of Finance has been behaving like a whirling dervish.
Then, in the fall of 1969, nearly two years after the previous minister of finance had pledged the white paper on taxation, we get a white paper on so-called tax reform which was presented to us as one of the finest conceptions of the human mind, about the greatest document since Magna Carta, backed by a tremendous public relations effort. Pretty soon criticism developed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is an old speech.
I would not want to cut off the parliamentary secretary because his time to interrupt anyone in the House is exceedingly limited.
Hear, hear!

Criticism of the white paper on tax reform developed very quickly. The minister portrayed himself as the guardian of the common people fighting the big interests, and fighting for reform required for the ordinary people in Canada. In the main he defended his proposals for about a year and a half, and then he capitulated. I have never seen a capitulation to equal this one in this country. To whom did he capitulate? Did he capitulate to the big interests who he said originally criticized the white paper?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.

Was it to the big interests that he capitulated? It is very difficult to say. I would hope not. The extent of the folly of the white paper on tax reform and the long defence conducted by the Minister of Finance, the extent of the abandonment of the basic concept put forward as being the fundamental wisdom, the whole business about narrowly and widely held corporations, the whole concept of the integration of corporate income and taxpayers income, were all abandoned. They talk about the time taken. They put forward a white paper on tax reform nearly two years after it was promised. They fought for it across the country for a year and a half, and then they abandoned most of it. When the Minister of Finance retreated last spring from the white paper I do not think there were many people on the other side of the House who thought he would retreat into something like this massive bill which we all have on our desks. I think it was as nasty a shock to them as it was to anybody else when it appeared.
Hear, hear!

So, I say that the time taken down to last June when the government retreated, and when it introduced this bill, was time taken by the government, nearly four years of time, first by the delay in putting forward a program of reform, and then by putting out a white paper on reform which was most inappropriate to conditions in Canada and which was nothing more than a technocrat's dream to which the government expected the Canadian economy and the Canadian people to conform, rather than a reform appropriate to the priorities and complexities of Canadian economy and life.
When the minister retreated, the master minds on the other side of the House produced Bill C-259, another technocratic creation. Now, we are involved with a new monstrosity. I do not want to be too hard on the private members opposite because I am sure they had no idea that after they had succeeded-because I think they played a part along with the rest of us-in forcing the Minister of Finance to retreat from the white paper that this would be hung round their necks.
So far as the time taken is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we have had years of procrastination to start with, years of delay, followed by years of the white paper and the present bill, years which I would describe as years of folly on the part of the government, consuming untold energy so far as the Canadian people are concerned, creating continual uncertainty in the country, and doing terrible damage to the economy of Canada.
Hear, hear!

Pushing this bill through now cannot be justified in the name of tax reform. It is true the government took years to produce this bill. It is true we have discussed it for many weeks. But that it was ill-conceived is apparent from its very length and bulk, from its complexity, from the incomprehensibility of many of its parts. That the government did not know what it was doing is shown in the number of amendments that the government
December 17, 1971

has produced this fall since the bill was introduced. There were some amendments very recently, and some amendments which the government has now promised it will have to pass to meet already recognized serious defects in the bill.
What does the Minister of Finance say, Mr. Speaker? In effect he says, "We don't know how badly this bill will work until we try it out on the Canadian people."
And the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says fuddle duddle.

Mr. Speaker, so far as the subject of tax reform is concerned, the Minister of Finance has been jumping around ever since he became Minister of Finance. He has been jumping around like a flea, if you can imagine it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: A funny looking flea.

As an example, I refer to the great fuss he made back in 1968 and 1969 about reforming estate and gift taxation, and the tremendous importance he attached to those changes at that time. Now, he has scrapped all that. When this bill comes into operation-I say when, not if, because I think the government is obviously determined to bull it through-there will be no estate or gift taxation imposed by the government. There will be no federal gift taxation or estate taxation.
I know some people have the impression that the recipient of a gift is the recipient of a capital gain, but that is completely erroneous, Mr. Speaker. There will be no gift taxation imposed upon a donor or donee under this bill. And no doubt, Sir, there will be hundreds of millions of dollars in Canada transferred or given away in the early part of 1972 because it will be possible to do so without any federal taxation.
They are looking after their rich contributors.

Yet in 1969, it was vitally important to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues that gifts should be taxed. It was basic to the tax philosophy of the government. One has to ask the question, Sir, when were the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance right, in 1968 and 1969 or in 1971? Were they right in proposing rigid, strict and complex tax laws with regard to gifts, putting this forward as a great tax reform two years ago, and now in what they describe as a great tax reform bill doing exactly the opposite, just within two years? When were they right, then or now? I say neither.
Clearly their behavior in putting forward this bill indicates they now think they were wrong in 1968 and 1969. And I think they are wrong in 1971. I doubt very much if any member on the other side of the House will rise to defend the taxation situation that will actually exist in 1972 with regard to gifts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We will.
Who has been wasting the time of the House and the country since 1969?

The Liberal party.
Income Tax Act

I just mention one example, the time taken by the government on estate and gift taxation. What about all the time spent on discussing the integration of corporate and shareholders' income, which the government has now completely abandoned? Again I ask, who has been wasting the time? But the saddest thing of all is not only that the government has wasted all this time but that we have wound up in the end with an abortion, if something the size of this bill could be called an abortion. If this bill passes this House today in its present form we will be making a pretty poor Christmas present to the Canadian people. It is the sort of package that not only won't look very good under the tree but it is liable to blow apart in the face of the person who opens it up.
The arguments have been gone over and over, Mr. Speaker, and there should be no need to repeat them today. There would not be any need if the government were willing to look at the situation with even a minimum amount of logic. I said it before, and I make no excuse for saying it here again because it is true, that most of this bill is incomprehensible, that much of it is irrelevant to the immediate problems facing the economy today; not only irrelevant but worse than that because when the bill comes into effect it will create a mountain of confusion in this country and in the economy of Canada, confusion this country can ill afford at this time. That is not the kind of present the government has any right to be giving to the Canadian people at the end of a session of Parliament.
Hear, hear!
Yesterday the Prime Minister said the bill was quite comprehensible to the taxpayers of Canada. If he were here, Sir, I would suggest to him: "Tell that to the tax experts, Buster."
Hear, hear!

Much of the bill is irrelevant, confusing and harmful. Indeed it is a sham. It is a sham because, after years of study, the Canadian people have a right to expect something that is tax reform rather than something that the government is calling tax reform. It is a sham because once the bill is passed the government will be able to make the claim that it has instituted tax reform when in fact it has done nothing of the kind. I say now, and I said before, that of course there are parts of the bill that are very welcome to everybody in this country. Basically, those are the parts which alleviate to some extent the burden on the lower income people of this country.
There are other provisions in the bill that deserve support, but you do not need this whole incomprehensible mess in order to achieve the things that are in the bill that are clearly of value. We have been willing and are still willing for the valuable aspects of this bill to go into effect immediately. It is a matter of simple justice and it would also add a stimulus to the economy. That is why I suggested splitting the bill for the purposes of proclaiming it and that is why I repeat that offer today. I am repeating it, Mr. Speaker. I think it is only sensible. When there are some points upon which there is agreement why not put them into effect? When there are other points on which even the government admits defects, and where even the government admits that changes have to be made, why not keep those points aside for future consideration and further

discussion? That is what the provinces request and it is the only sensible course in order to avoid a tax jungle in this country. It would seem to be the logical way to proceed.
I suggest that this tax legislation has one thing in common with a good bottle of wine-the longer it stays unopened the better it will be for all concerned. I think our suggestions is the logical way to proceed but I would hardly expect a government preoccupied with claiming political points to worry very much about logic or common sense. Beyond logical procedure, this government is not even concerned about the parliamentary procedure. After brutally stopping debate in this House, this government is now stepping on all the toes it can find to stop the debate in the other place before that debate has even started.
Just like it is denying the people of N ewf o undland.
That is what you call a really good dose of participatory democracy.
Just like their treatment of the poor, if you speak up you get your grants cut off.
Who is making the speech?
Let your leader speak, George. You will have your chance.
We are able to participate over here; it is a joint effort.
Hear, hear!
We are allowed to speak, we are not muzzled like you are.

It needs to be a joint effort over here when the government seems to be determined to walk on the face of everybody they can find. Consider the effrontery. It does not surprise me that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) would do this because it is his natural disposition, but consider the effrontery of the government when it presents the Senate with this tax bill, presumably later today-
After two years with the people.

-and says it must go into effect on January 1. As I said, Mr. Speaker, the attitude of the Minister of National Defence does not surprise me at all, I would only be surprised if he were to take a different attitude.
Why don't you tell the truth?
I cannot think of anything more insulting to the other place, or of any effort by any government more designed to try to reduce the role of the other place to that of a farce.
Poor old Paul Martin!
Nobody in a non-elected body should ever tell an elected body what to do.

speechtext: May we have order, please. The hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, if I were a Liberal Senator right now, which of course I am not and it is something I could never hope to be, I would be considering not my status in the party, I hope-

-I would be considering my reputation as a member of that institution, which has a record of some independence and should be particularly anxious to maintain it at this time.

Despite some of the comments opposite, this is not a question of a non-elected body trying to hold up the will of an elected body in this country, Mr. Speaker. This House has been prevented by closure from examining this bill fully.

Black Friday again.
It is sad, Mr. Speaker. There are many sad aspects of this whole thing and the saddest is the frustration of hon. gentlemen opposite.

You sail your hydrofoil, Don.

The only time I see any sign of vitality in the hon. gentleman is when he is trying to push somebody around.

When he is trying to get his hydrofoil off the water.
Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, the Senate does not have to run according to any strict timetable set by my hon. friends opposite. I hope it will not permit itself to be tied down to some political timetable that this government has prescribed. I hope it does not do that, Mr. Speaker.
Last Monday I explained why we were opposed to this bill and I will do so again.
That is repetition. It does not do any good.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
You would know all about repetition.
Please listen to Mr. Speaker.
Make it perfectly clear.
Don't get pushed aside by a mosquito.
I don't think it is fair to compare a mosquito to the hon. member.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which does nothing for the Canadian economy. I want to repeat, there are aspects of the bill that are desirable from every point of view, including stimulus to the economy, but the bulk of this bill does absolutely nothing for the Canadian economy.
Hear, hear!

It does nothing to help it. It is a bill that can adversely affect federal-provincial relations in this country. The two largest provinces in the country have asked for deferment, time to study, time to adjust and presumably time to make further representation after they succeed in understanding the bill. It is a bill that, in large measure, has been badly thought out and obviously badly drafted in view of the number of amendments that have been introduced, and badly presented. This bill, in the interest of the Canadian people, must be thought out again in large measure to ensure that it does not further damage the sense of initiative and the spirit of incentive upon which this country depends. We need tax reform in the interests of justice; we need it in the interests of economic progress; we need it in the interests of our national independence; and we certainly need to consider tax reform in the interests of ensuring full employment.
Again, I say, that is our No. 1 priority in this country. There are vast sections of this bill which not only do not help in the employment situation but which will discourage and militate against successful efforts to bring about full employment in this country. We may very well need tax reform in the interests of justice, independence and economic progress, but much of this bill, Sir, we just do not need. Above all we do not need and do not want a bill which will compound and increase confusion and uncertainty in this country.
That, in summary, is why I oppose this bill and that is why I support the amendment before the House at this
Income Tax Act
time. I hope all other hon. members will do likewise, Mr. Speaker, and that even at the eleventh hour reasonable members on the government side will resist the despotic tendencies of the Minister of Finance and others in the government. I hope they will consider their position, accept the proposal, which is sensible, for splitting the bill for purposes of proclamation and thereby serve the country rather than trying to serve themselves.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am rising to participate on this last day of debate on the tax bill, partly because it is the last day and partly because of the number of issues of a parliamentary character that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) raised in his speech. The government, to my knowledge, has never accused the opposition of wasting time, and neither has the country.
Oh, oh!
Then, what is the purpose of the government's motion?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Neither the government nor the country have accused the opposition of wasting time in discussing the all important question of tax reform. We, on this side of the House, believe that the passing of this bill will put an end to the uncertainty which bothers the Leader of the Opposition.
What about the amendment?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We also believe that the passing of the bill will restore and produce greater equity in our taxing system, and that it will provide for greater growth and employment in the country.
Hear, hear!
What about the amendments?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Speaking on the merits of the bill may I say that we, on this side of the House, are satisfied that we have produced the best possible product as a result of-

However, I want to get back to the amendment.
The amendment has been moved in all solemnity by the official opposition and today, in the final address made to the House by the Leader of the Opposition, he calls upon us to support that amendment. It is a motion of non-confidence in the government. If that amendment were carried we would be defeated and we do not intend to support that amendment. Not only would we be defeated, but the tax bill would probably be defeated. I want to tell the House why we cannot accept the amendment.
First of all, it is an incredible amendment. It belies any proper belief in the capacity of the opposition to formulate any reasonable proposition for the consideration of the House. For example, if this amendment were accepted, the provisions that we developed and which were approved in committee for the co-operatives and credit unions would not come into effect. Members of the official opposition have been crying to the government, and mem-

bers of the NDP party have been crying to the government, to bring in new provisions. We did. We brought in good provisions which have been accepted by the co-operatives and credit unions. speechtext: I suggest to the minister that this is debate between members. Mr. Speaker, the NDP will not be able to support the amendment before the House for two reasons. The first is that to the extent that it might be effective, and there is considerable doubt that it would be, it is a tremendous act of favouritism; second, it is probably not effective in the least, and therefore makes no sense and has no meaning in the examination of the bill before us.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) seemed to have directed his chief attack against the official opposition and seemed to have looked at this corner with some degree of favour. I am sorry that we will not be able to reciprocate. This debate has taken on the aspect of an auction sale between the Liberal and the Conservative parties to see who can give this country away faster to big business. It has been a complete disgrace. If we were to examine the course of this debate, read the minutes of the committee-and those volumes make a pile almost three or four feet high-we would see how much attention has been devoted to the problems of the ordinary taxpayer in this country, and how many briefs have been presented to the committee that dealt with the ordinary taxpayers of Canada. There were not many such briefs. If you were to examine Hansard, and I have not had a chance to comb through each line because it would be such a tremendous task, you would see how many words by either the government or the official opposition have been devoted to the problems of the ordinary people in this country and how many speeches were directed toward the problems of big business in Canada. There is a smell of an election in the air, and both the Liberals and the Conservatives are
Income Tax Act
falling over each other to see who can most please the bagmen of the giant industries who pay their expenses. I know I am being political, but I also know that this is a political arena.
The unions are paying your way.

I am quite happy to have the unions pay our way. I am quite happy to receive whatever donations the unions wish to give to this party.
When I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) yesterday delivering one of his rare speeches I noted that in three of his opening paragraphs he used the word "fair" at least six times in a desperate attempt to convince himself-he was not convincing anyone else-that the just society he talked about was being supported by this tax bill. In my view those words were hollow; they had no meaning whatsoever, and simply using the word "fair" does not make this bill fair at all. Essentially, we are continuing the same kind of tax system we have always had. The Liberal party does not need the Conservatives in to tell them of the dangers facing the country in trying to tax business. The Liberals have their own backbenchers who will do that. They have been running to the minister and making him back off from any such provision contained in the legislation. People in this country who have hoped for some significant tax reform cannot help but be disappointed with the bill that will come to a vote later on this day.
After nine years of study, reports and discussions, Canada has wound up with a tax system which is still grossly unfair and bears much too heavily on the lower and middle income groups. It does that, not because we have to tax these groups so heavily for government revenues but because we are giving benefits to many people, to the resource industries and to the investors of this country in order to make their lot in life much easier.
Last evening we heard the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans) indicate the significant tax savings that could be effected, how rates could be lowered for the middle and lower income groups if special tax privileges were taken away from the mining and resource industries and the investors of Canada. To the extent that these benefits are being given to the privileged groups in Canada, every wage and salary earner must pay considerably more than the government is entitled to ask of him or her. We are continuing the system under the present legislation. The principles that the NDP endorses are ones of equity and redistribution of income. They have been watered down in successive reports, and in the Benson bill now before Parliament they have virtually been nullified.
I can well remember in the early stages the bold, brave Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). I believed then, and I still believe today, that the Minister of Finance really wanted to see a genuine tax reform in this country. People often ask me, who do you think is the villain in the piece? It is fashionable to paint the pipe smoking Minister of Finance as the villain in the piece. He is the one who did away with tax reform. He is the one toward whom all ire has been directed. But I think that in the early days there was a real wish on the part of this man to bring in genuine tax reform, but there was no rapport between him and his party and pressures were continually being brought on

December 17, 1971
Income Tax Act
him within his own party. His own backbenchers were going across the country saying how terrible this tax reform bill was, how they were going to do something about it, assuring their business supporters "do not worry, we will get to Benson and we will make him back off". They did get to the Minister of Finance and he has backed off.
The initial reforms were not significant to begin with, and the continuous watering down of those reforms has left us with a meaningless document which does nothing to further the cause of equity and fairness in our society. We have the lightweight capital gains tax. This government takes great pride in having brought in the capital gains tax and now they are bringing in arguments to show how useful this tax will be. This is the last country in the industrialized world which does not have a capital gains tax, and now they are taking pride in having introduced it. It is only a half-gains tax. If a person gets his income from wages or salaries, if he works for his income in one way or another, he has to pay tax on every single cent that he earns. But if he has a lot of money, either left to him or available to him, money which he can invest, he is spared the cost of giving his share to the tax collector. He has to pay on only half of that money. We say, in effect, that it is far nobler to collect money that way and that therefore we will reward the man who obtains his income in that way. If he works for it one way or another, either in a white or a blue collar job, if he sweeps the floor in a factory or teaches university students, he pays tax on every cent he earns.
But if a man is an investor, then he does not have to pay the same rate of tax. If he is even more fortunate and happens to have invested in the oil or mining industries, then his rate of tax is even lower. We say to him, that is great; go ahead and put your money in these industries and we will give you a special tax break. Yet, evidence is mounting that these industries are responsible for destroying our potential for growth in this country. Whatever benefit they may have brought, whatever justification there might have been for tax concessions in the early stages of the development of Canada-and I will not argue that there were no benefits from them and that there were no reasons for encouraging this kind of investment-there is no longer such justification.
We are a nation of 22 million people who desperately need to find jobs for almost 300,000 new entrants a year into our labour force, and we cannot find them if the emphasis continues to be on resource development. It would be bad enough if the tax system were completely neutral and we were still heavily emphasizing resource development. But to have a high level of unemployment, such as we have now, and to see young people coming into the labour force for the first time seeking jobs, and in the face of this to encourage the resource industries by tax concessions is positively insane. One wonders how any government could have brought in provisions of this kind, or could have failed to see the merit in reducing such benefits to the resource industries.
It can be argued that while the national interest would call for a diminution of encouragement to resource development, there are some provinces that need such develop-

ment. This is a good argument. It is one I accept. But we have two choices. We can either say, "We are going to do this in the national interest regardless of the consequences to individual provinces," or say something that would be more fair, namely, that to the extent that any province is disadvantaged as a result of our taking action in the national interest, we will see to it that the revenues of the country are shared equally.
In that event, we would change our tax sharing agreements between the federal government and the provincial governments. We would secure the increase in manufacturing that we think needs to occur, and the increase in the service industries that we think needs to occur in order to provide jobs for our young people, and distribute the resultant increase in tax revenues all across the land so that there would not be a feeling of dissatisfaction. The people in the west would no longer see the actions taken as being only for the benefit of Ontario. We would have to make the case that they were for the benefit of the entire nation. Those are the kinds of tax sharing agreements that we should have. Unfortunately, we do not have them at the moment. The sell-out to the resource industry lobby is particularly shocking at this time because, Mr. Speaker, in the first place the government did not intend to do very much. The result is that the resource industries are almost back to enjoying the advantages they had at the beginning.
I can remember when estate tax legislation was discussed in the House of Commons. Today I listened to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), a man for whom I have a great deal of respect, and I wondered at his rather short memory of that debate. But maybe I just did not understand the hon. gentleman. It seemed to me as though he was deploring the fact that the federal government had dropped its role in estate taxation. That sounded a little strange. I know that many of the people in the Conservative party were quite happy to see the federal government get out of the field of estate taxation. I also know they will be happy to see the provinces get out of that field. But then I heard that the Leader of the Opposition is far more progressive than some of his followers. That is something I can understand. However, we should not forget that debate and the vigorous fight put up by the Conservative party against any increases or adjustments in estate taxes.
It is foolish to stand up in this House and cry over the fact that the federal government is getting out of the estate tax field. I think it is wrong for the federal government to get out of that field, and in an earlier speech I said that the decision to do so was made in an absent-minded fit of pique. The federal government was not deriving much revenue from that tax, and it got mad at the provinces. It asked, "Why should we collect this for the provinces? Let them stew in their own juices. Let them collect their own estate taxes." This will have an adverse effect on federal-provincial co-operation. This shattered egg will have to be restored in a new form. As other hon. members have pointed out, there will be a tremendous transfer of wealth take place when this legislation comes into effect.
Tax relief for old age pensioners and the immediate removal of some taxpayers from the rolls are a long-overdue recognition by the government that it should stop robbing the poor. This relief will do little more than par-
December 17, 1971

tially compensate those taxpayers for their losses through inflation in recent years. The other day my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), made a fine contribution to this tax debate when he pointed out that the increase in exemptions was not even equivalent to the rise in inflation that has taken place since the last time the exemption levels were set.
Not only does the outcome of this tax debate leave us with a most unsatisfactory income and wealth tax structure, but nothing has been done to end the regressiveness of our tax system. Greater recognition of the financial requirements of the provinces, which are facing the growing costs of urbanization, educational and social needs, should have been a first step in any kind of tax reform. Almost nothing has been done in that area.
I would like to make another point about the taxation of resources. When the federal government abdicates its role to tax new resource industries at the same level as it taxes manufacturing, it must be remembered that the resource industries are not completely exempted from tax. The situation is not quite as it appears on the surface because resource industries do pay tax, although perhaps not as much as they should. The question then must be asked, to whom should they pay this tax? Should it be to the federal government which has a redistribution program which in fact takes wealth from some of the richer provinces and makes it available to the poorer provinces? Should it be to the provinces, under a tax system which permits the wealthier provinces to keep the bulk of the wealth for themselves? To the extent that the federal government abdicates its role to tax resource industries, it provides an opportunity for provincial governments to move in and take the lion's share of this tax wealth, which is not distributed but is used by the individual provinces concerned. This is a way for the richer provinces to avoid the responsibility that they have to the poorer provinces. Sharing does not take place to the extent that it should.
We have been very critical throughout this whole debate, and we think we have had good cause to be critical. But in summing up at the close of the debate, we do not want to leave simply the criticism. We also made many constructive proposals. We made many suggestions as to the shape that the country's tax system should have. I would like to summarize our views on the kind of tax system we would like for Canada.
First, we think a comprehensive income concept has to be adopted, with all forms of economic gain to be included and subjected to a graduated scale of income tax based on ability to pay. There has to be an elimination of the traditional double standard in our system. Taxes should be based on a person's ability to pay rather than on how he derives his income. We see no justification for saying that this kind of income will be taxed at one rate, another kind of income at another rate, and that a third kind of income will receive special preferential treatment. That is unfair. We accept the Carter Commission proposal that all income be taxed on the same basis.
Second, capital gains should be taxed at full rates, rather than at the half rates proposed in the bill, on realization, in the same way as salaries, wages and other forms of income, with adequate provision for averaging, exemptions for the family home and farm home, and safeguards to prevent the break-up of family farms and
Income Tax Act
small businesses when passed on to sons and daughters. We look around this country, which has been more than generous in its tax system and tax treatment to business, and we see the results of that kind of favouritism. This country has the highest level of foreign ownership of any country in the world and, to a large extent, the tax system is to blame for that. The absence of a capital gains tax in Canada has encouraged our business men to sell out rather than operate their business because they could make a profit on which they paid no tax, but if they continued to operate they would have to pay tax.
We have offered a 20 per cent dividend tax credit to investors in the vain hope that these financial incentives would encourage Canadian ownership but that has failed. The pace of foreign acquisition is the greatest in the world.
It is an awfully good idea.
You like foreign investment?

You would recommend a full capital gains tax, yet you are against foreign investment. You cannot have it both ways. You cannot take all the capital gains from Canadians, and then cry about foreign investment; that is the anomaly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member is making a speech while remaining seated. That is not in accordance with the Standing Orders or any kind of order.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I got involved in a little argument.

I am glad to see that the hon. member was paying attention to the debate, although I might say he was not paying much attention to the economy as the peculiar logic he has expressed demonstrates.
We in the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, also believe there should be a system of tax credits instead of exemptions, because exemptions provide better benefits to those with higher incomes while tax credit makes it easier to maintain equity when making tax changes.
As a fourth point, we believe in the removal of unjustified tax concessions for natural resource industries, especially concessions relating to depletion allowances.
As a fifth point, we want to see strict limits on corporation capital cost allowances, advertising, entertainment and convention expenses. Some might argue that this is what the government is attempting but there is no real indication that they have made any substantial advance in curbing the excessive costs, despite the new legislation.
As a sixth point, we want to see the removal of the dividend tax credit, since it mainly benefits upper income groups and is not necessarily an incentive to growth. Abolition of the much abused dual rate, but adoption of other provisions to assist small businesses in obtaining credit, is desirable.
Throughout debate we have tried to make the point that there should be substantial assistance to small businesses trying to get established. We need more businesses, more entrepreneurship in Canada and that assistance should be forthcoming. We do not believe the way to do it is to

December 17, 1971
Income Tax Act
reward businesses after they have made money, which is what the present tax system does; we believe it should be done through incentives and encouragement when those businesses need help the most. The present system is a "give away" program rather than a real assistance to business, and we think it is the wrong kind of incentive and works against the idea of assisting genuine small businesses which are trying to grow.
As a seventh point, we believe the same treatment for employment expenses should be allowed for wage and salary earners as is now allowed for the self-employed, plus tax credits for the cost of child care. The government proposes a $150 employment expense deduction. That is unsatisfactory, since in a few cases it might be too much but in most cases it is inadequate. Many employees incur expenses in excess of this amount. There are many special cases and extraordinary expenses which will not be met by this provision. When we contract that with the generous provisions for the self-employed who are allowed to deduct all the costs, we find the system grossly unfair.
The argument put forth by the government is not an objection to the principle of equity. They agree that the system is inequitable. They accept the argument that the treatment of the self-employed is much better than the treatment of employees, and that something should be done about it, but they offer the argument of administrative efficiency. They say that since there are many more employees than self-employed, it is not practical to examine the tax returns of every employee to permit them to include legitimate expenses. That is a spurious argument, Mr. Speaker, and surely a disgrace to any tax system. To say that it cannot be done because it is not easy or is not convenient will not be accepted by those persons being harmed under the system. Either we have a tax system which provides that everyone will be limited to a certain amount or we have a tax system which accepts legitimate employment expenses incurred by both the self-employed and employees, and we examine their tax returns to that end. Other countries do this, so surely it is not beyond the administrative ability of the Canadian government to work some kind of equity into our tax system.
As an eighth point, we think inheritances and gifts should be subject to a tax levy which would be paid by the recipient, not by the donor, to ensure that the state receives a fair share when transfers between generations occur. Particular arrangements would be made to prevent undue hardship when family farms or small businesses are transferred from parents to children. It does not seem that much argument can be made against an inheritance tax in our society. If a man's individual efforts were responsible for the creation of growth without any assistance from society, his employees or any of the other organizations that exist, there might be an argument against inheritance tax on the wealth to be passed on. But we know this is untrue; in our civilized society people cannot operate without assistance from each other. Business today is probably the largest recipient of benefits from the government. There are many programs for assistance and there is the provision of fire and police services, of roads and transportation networks, so there is a social input. Land does not increase in value simply because it sits there; it increases in value because of the social conditions which contribute to the growth of a

country. For those reasons, I think that the government of a country has a claim on part of the wealth that is created. I do not think there should be too much objection, if that claim is a fair one, if some of it is paid to the government and the other people in the country, upon death.
Mr. Speaker, nine years ago many of us looked forward to seeing genuine tax reform and the events of the last couple of years have been a grave disappointment. We had hoped that the Carter commission, with its superb logic, its well documented cases, would have some influence on the minds of those in government. It has had little or no influence at all.
The thrust of the debate in this House was not to the effect that the government was being far too timid in implementing tax reform. The thrust was in the opposition direction. It was suggested that the government was being far too progressive. Committees like the Committee on Fair Taxation spent enormous sums of money trying to persuade the ordinary people of Canada that the new tax system would be too socialistic. The business community rose as a group and attacked the modicum of tax reform there is in the bill and said that the bill is too socialistic. Unfortunately, between elections, the ordinary people are not organized to make representations on this subject. It is our hope that at the next election they will cast their judgments and thereby say that this tax bill constitutes a sabotage of tax reform.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I begin by saying that points of the kind just made by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) have been previously raised and, I think, effectively rebutted by other speakers on behalf of the government earlier in the debate. None of his arguments can remove the fact that the government's proposals will bring about lower taxes for millions of Canadians, particularly those in the lower income groups. Therefore, these proposals deserve the support of the House at this time. Mr. Speaker, now that Parliament appears to be moving closer to the point of final decision on tax reform legislation, I think that the House would expect me to say something-
Hear, hear!
Say something.

-about the way the Department of National Revenue will approach the task of its administration of
December 17, 1971

the new law when it receives final parliamentary approval and royal assent.
Any task of administration, Mr. Speaker, is, of course, governed by the provisions of the law in question. But it is unrealistic to expect that tax laws, both those which have been on the statute books for years and, more particularly, new laws such as we are considering now can be drafted so perfectly that there is no room for differing interpretations of them in some circumstances. Despite the best of intentions, it is inevitable that there are ambiguities to be resolved in the interpretation of laws of this kind. Therefore, in deciding upon an official interpretation the Department of National Revenue is guided by legal advisers and by considerations of reasonableness and practicality.
However, where two interpretations seem to have equal support, having regard to equity, reasonableness, statutory interpretation and the general intent of the legislation as a whole, the interpretation is adopted which gives the benefit of the doubt to the taxpayer. This is already the department's policy under the present law. I want to assure the House that this will certainly be the policy of the department when it starts applying the many new provisions contained in the bill which is presently before us, once, of course, it receives final parliamentary approval.
The underlying philosophy of the taxation division of the department, as hon. members know, has been evolving over the past several years to take account of increased taxpayer interest and participation in the process of tax administration. The main thrust of these changes has been in the direction of the most complete possible dissemination of taxation information to all taxpayers and the establishment of better communications between taxpayer and the department. When it adopted this approach the department knew it would likely be faced with the job of administering a new tax statute.
We recognized, of course, that in spite of efforts not to have them, inevitably there would be problems in adjusting to a new tax system, both for the taxpayer and the tax administrator. We have therefore been trying to anticipate what the major problems might be and to plan our administrative practices with a view to minimizing any possible difficulties for the taxpayer and the department.
The department acknowledges the inherent right of the taxpayer to all the information and all the assistance that it can give him. As well, it realizes that if its administrative mechanism is in any way high-handed, it is only adding to the problems of administration. The department cannot expect a taxpayer to accord it the co-operation it requires to maintain the efficiency and integrity of our voluntary compliance system if it does not extend the fullest co-operation to him. The department, therefore, intends to make a very special effort to ensure that the needs of the taxpayer under the new tax system are met fully and sympathetically. Therefore, I would like to describe to the House some of the steps we will be taking to assist taxpayers in the adjustment period to try to achieve as smooth a transition as possible from the old to the proposed new tax system.
While there are other measures which I shall describe later in my remarks, let me speak first about the public 24725-41
Income Tax Act
information program on the new law the department will begin to administer once the law receives royal assent. The department will be centering this public information program around a series of pamphlets covering the various topics of tax reform. In our view, this is the most effective way to handle material of this complexity. These printed publications are being written in as simple language as possible and in a form which is concise and to the point.
To lessen the possibility of confusion, the department has developed a selective mailing system so that most taxpayers will receive only the information they will want and require. Groups of taxpayers have been selected from our computer master file and direct mail packages containing topics affecting each group will be mailed, using computer-generated address labels. These publications will also be advertised nationally as being available from our head office or any of our 28 district taxation offices. The advertising messages will serve those taxpayers who for whatever reason are not on the tax roll, those who may mislay the publications they receive through the mail and those who cannot be selected as a distinct group.
In summary, what the department is endeavouring to do is give each taxpayer in every walk of life sufficient printed information in understandable terms so that he will be able to be aware of the changes brought about by the new law. What the department is trying to avoid is the flooding of the taxpayer's mail with information that he would not likely consider to be relevant and useful to him.
I would like to give the House more details of this publication program. Eleven pamphlets have been planned, each dealing with a different subject, and there will be additions to the list if the need arises. These subjects are: Highlights for individuals, Valuation Day, Child Care Expenses, Moving Expenses, Capital Gains, Partnerships, Rental Income and Undeveloped Land, Goodwill and Similar Assets, the Professions-Income Calculation, Basic Herds, and Corporate Tax Guide.
I have referred to the groups of taxpayers which will be selected from the computer master file. The groups are: married women, businessmen, professionals, farmers, rental property owners, corporations, and all other individuals. Each of these groups, some of which of course will overlap, will receive a package of pamphlets of direct interest, although some of the printed publications such as Valuation Day and Highlights for Individuals will go to most groups.
I will not take the time of the House to describe all the publications in detail, but it may be of interest to hon. members if I give some explanation of two of the pamphlets that I have mentioned, Highlights for Individuals, and Valuation Day. The Valuation Day pamphlet will attempt to achieve two purposes. First, it will point out in simple language that most people will not be affected by Valuation Day, and others may or may not be affected initially. This message will be prominently displayed on the first page. Taxpayers who are affected will be invited to read on, to find out what action they should take. As the publication will make clear, such action will be in their interest, and the bulk of the text will be used to explain this.

December 17, 1971
Income Tax Act
The pamphlet entitled Highlights for Individuals will outline all major changes that may affect the individual taxpayer. In addition, the taxpayer will be informed as to whether any immediate action is required on his part. If so, he will be directed by the text to one of the specialized pamphlets to which I referred earlier in my remarks.
It sounds easy.

If not, the text will inform him that further information on how to file will be forwarded with his return and guide when it becomes necessary and he will be informed this will not be necessary until filing time in the early part of 1973.
Hon. members will have observed that in referring to pamphlet titles I have not mentioned a number of subjects of tax reform. In most instances, these are subjects that are of interest to a minority of taxpayers. We have planned to treat those subjects by the issuance of information circulars which will go on our regular mailing list and be available in our district offices, rather than publish separate pamphlets which would be required in comparatively small numbers. The department has tried to anticipate all the requirements for printed information. But, as I indicated earlier, the situation will be watched closely and if it appears other subjects should be dealt with by specialized pamphlets, resources will be available to act immediately.
We believe the distribution of these publications will serve to answer the vast majority of questions that will occur to taxpayers. At the same time, we realize that we can never anticipate all the questions and problems that may arise. As an additional means of providing increased assistance to taxpayers during the early stages of implementation of the new law, we are establishing a new informal consultation service.
I have mentioned that the taxation component of the Department of National Revenue has 28 district offices across Canada. We have one of the most highly decentralized departments of government, with 85 per cent of our taxation employees situated in the district offices to provide direct service to the public. Each district office now maintains an inquiry service. Taxpayers may inquire at the counter, telephone or write for information. Last year, for instance, these offices dealt with more than two million such inquiries. With the advent of tax reform, this service is being expanded and improved.
Taxpayers may visit, telephone or write their own district office for information. In most instances our regular information staff, augmented as the need arises, will be able to answer questions arising out of the new law. But some taxpayers will have difficult problems dealing, for instance, with a complex business operation. These taxpayers will be referred by the regular information staff to our informal consultation service which will be staffed by officers in each district office with special training and who will be particularly well informed about the new legislation. These expert advisers, in turn, will be in ready touch by telephone with a central group of experts in head office. As soon as an answer can be provided by this informal consultation service, the taxpayer will be contacted by telephone or by the quickest possible means. In 
this way we will be able to provide a relatively fast answering service for difficult problems, consistent with a proper consideration of them by knowledgeable taxation employees.
This advice will not be binding on the department but will merely be the best opinion that can be given without the detailed documentation that would be required for a binding advance income tax ruling. The aim is to provide the best quick service that we can. I referred earlier to efforts of the department to establish better lines of communication with the taxpayer so as to remove as far as possible the uncertainty as to his position under the law. One of several steps in that direction was the inauguration of an advance ruling system under which the department provides rulings binding on the department as long as the relevant law remains unchanged.
When I spoke to the Tax Foundation in Vancouver a few weeks ago I said it had been incorrectly reported in the press that the department will not give binding advance rulings under the proposed new law once it came into effect. Let me again confirm that these reports were not correct. The department will continue to give these rulings once the new law goes into effect, subject only to the same limitations and qualifications as in the past.
I know that many taxpayers are relying on the availability of this service to assist them in removing uncertainties. I have therefore directed that every effort must be made to expand the staff of the department's rulings division. This is being done in an endeavour to meet the concern about the degree of delay in the issuing of rulings that may be caused by the volume and complexity of the requests for them. The rulings division staff will be augmented with experienced officers from the district taxation offices and other branches at head office on a loan basis as well as by the recruitment of some additional personnel on a permanent basis. By these means there will be an expansion of about 50 per cent in the number of experienced accountants engaged in this work. As a result, we now anticipate that advance income tax rulings will be obtainable under the proposed new law, once it receives royal assent, within approximately the same span of time that they have been obtained under the present law.
It is certainly incumbent on the tax administrator to offer every assistance to taxpayers, especially when the laws are revised or new measures are introduced. I want to repeat that the department is most anxious to help taxpayers in every walk of life to become familiar with the new law in the form it is passed by Parliament. As a further means of trying to be helpful, the department is planning a series of special briefings in convenient locations across the country.
Some professional organizations have already held seminars on tax reform and others will be holding tax conferences in the months ahead. These meetings and the information disseminated by these organizations are of great assistance to their members. But there are other taxpayers and tax practitioners in relatively small practices who do not have such means of acquainting themselves with the new law. For the benefit of these taxpayers and for private practitioners or consultants who help them prepare their returns but who feel they are not able to get adequate information through professional organi-
December 17, 1971

zations, we are proposing to hold special tax reform briefings in various communities. Videotape recordings and other such aids will be used at these briefings to explain the new law, and taxation officers will be in attendance to answer questions.
We propose to hold these briefings after the 1972 filing season has ended, that is, from next May on. Prior to that time taxpayers will be concerned primarily with filing under the present law and practitioners will be similarly engaged.
Whenever Parliament amends the Income Tax Act it is necessary to establish a definite starting date for the new or revised provisions in the law.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the minister, but it is my duty to do so. As His Honour mentioned earlier today, under the new Standing Order there is an informal arrangement that I know all hon. members will want to follow.

Mr. Speaker, with the limited time at my disposal I will try to cover some of the points I want to make. The speech of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) is what we expect from this particular member, certainly from a coastal constituency: it is filled with red herrings.
Hear, hear!

Some have been answered by my colleagues, but the remarks dealing with the amendment are the reddest and most odorous of all.
We have used a simple device on third reading to send the bill back to committee of the whole to review the proposal for splitting the bill, a proposal which has received universal approval from all over this land, from people in business, farming, industry and the press. Only the Liberals have rejected it. We do not seek to bind the hands of the committee as to the exact means of division. But our views are known and accepted. What we want is a division on lines acceptable to the country.
Hear, hear!

I believe one of the saddest spectacles I have seen in this Parliament was the night the tax reform bill of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was passed in the House, 75 clauses, with less than one-quarter of the book of 735 pages reviewed. It required over 135 amendments to deal with corrections to this one-quarter that was reviewed. On the same basis, it would require well over 400 amendments to correct the whole of the bill.
A complex and complicated bill that even the tax accountants and tax lawyers could not understand was passed in a period of 3j hours. The Members of Parliament were robots, forced to bow to a majority government run by a modern dictatorship. The hysteria of the cockpit was nothing compared with Parliament that night.
Hear, hear!

The government argued as its reason for bringing in closure that over 40 days were taken up with discussion and that was long enough. Mr. Speaker, what has that to do with it? The bill should be properly
Income Tax Act
analysed on the floor of this House until it has been understood and until all of it has been reviewed.
One might accept the government's premise if the bill had been the usual short one, containing a few pages, but this was a 737-page document which required 137 amendments in a quarter of its length. To show the complexity of this legislation I am tabling an article by Marshall, Russell and White that bears this point out. Surely, the point has been entirely missed. Whether it required 10 days or 100 days for consideration is irrelevant. What matters is that it should be adequately discussed. In fact, the House and the committee of the whole made progress with reasonable speed by comparison with the time taken to consider other bills.
In any case, the government could have agreed to divide this long, ponderous bill, separating the non-contentious areas which were easily understood. But they flatly refused to do this. The government alone must accept responsibility for the fact that almost three-quarters of the measure has been forced through the House by closure. This was done despite the pleas of the Senate committee and the various other groups and institutions which counselled against approving parts of the legislation, and the wishes of the five Premiers who urged the government not to proceed with it. Incidentally, two of these Premiers represent the provinces of Ontario and Quebec which between them contain 75 per cent of the population of Canada. Perhaps the only analogy we have is the Domesday Bill put through by William the Conqueror almost 900 years ago.
In defence of these proposals, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made one of his infrequent speeches in this chamber during which he referred to the million people he was taking off the tax rolls. Mr. Speaker, those people should have been taken off long ago. Inflation, set off by this government, has proceeded at such a pace that the government was obliged to take this action. They had been asked over and over again by the opposition to do so, but they refused to act until they had no choice. This section could have been passed two months ago, three months ago, six months ago or two years ago. But the government did nothing about it. Now they put this little sugar pill in with all these other provisions. It is bitter aloes, though, because it should have come much sooner. They should have done this three years ago.
Members opposite claim that the press are behind them. They say their actions are supported by editorial writers. I wish to read from the Globe and Mail, Canada's national newspaper, which had this to say:
What the government is saying to all of us is this: swallow what we hand you whether you understand it or not, or we'll use closure to make you swallow it. How bad this will be with the tax bill we cannot know till it hits us. But if the government employs the same tactics with the Competition Act and with legislation to control foreign and even Canadian investment, then both the economy that supports us and the freedoms we enjoy could be at grave risk. What has been proposed would deny many rights to individuals and could plunge us into depression. But if we ask for time to argue the points, the government can slap on closure and make us, in a very real sense, its prisoners.
What we are fighting is not any longer the tax bill-bad as it may be-but this arrogant use of closure to shut Parliament and people out of the running of their own affairs.
