Now, Mr. Speaker, just to set the record straight, may I remind the House that as reported in Hansard at page 2162 on March 26, 1962, my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) introduced a motion to do away with closure. He had this to say:
All of us agree that full and free debate is necessary in the parliamentary system, the examination without restraint of the programs and policies advanced not only by the government but by those in the opposition who would provide an alternative government. In the process of national decision-making the role of Parliament is pre-eminent and vital. I believe, in the light of the experience of the past, that the principle of closure need no longer be accepted under our system-
We in Parliament have a duty to preserve the freedom of debate because our freedom, the freedom of parliament, is essential to the freedom of the people we represent. When we have rules that confine or limit our freedom in debate we are permitting rules that also limit freedom in Canada outside Parliament as well.
Then he went on to refer to a statement by Mr. Ernest Lapointe:
It is the will of Parliament, not that of the government, that is the will of the nation.
If the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) has anything to say, let him get up and say it and not keep talking from his seat, as is a habit of his. Now I wish to read what Mr. Mackenzie King had to say on the same subject:
I want to make it perfectly clear that the battle which has been put up in connection with this measure is not merely over the rights of minorities or the rights of majorities; it is true that it has to do with the rights of both, rights which in the case of the majority no less than in that of the minority, are threatened.
Next I wish to read what Mr. Pickersgill had to say. He was one of the prominent members of this House. He learned his lesson, and this ought to be required reading for all members on the other side:
I believe that no government in its senses would ever again use the existing closure rule in our book. I therefore do not see any sense in leaving it there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Did you buy that?

I shall now put on record what the Winnipeg Tribune has to say about contempt for Parliament.
In the 1969 summer session, the Trudeau government delivered a one-two sneak punch to freedom of debate in the House of Commons. The government invoked closure to choke off debate on a bill that gave it even more drastic powers of closure-the notorious Bill 75c.
At the time Donald Macdonald, the Liberal House leader, contended that 75c would never be used to limit debate to the minimum allowed on a major bill. Today the Trudeau government is using 75c to choke off discussion of its 707-page tax bill before the first 200 pages of the measure have been given clause-by-clause scrutiny.
So much for assurances by autocrats that they will never use autocratic powers. And so much for Ron Basford's soothing assurances that the harsh provisions of his Competition Act will not be invoked.
During the 1969 debate, Prime Minister Trudeau made it clear that he regarded MPs on opposition benches as a bunch of nobodies. He made the smart-alec comment that the IQ of the Commons rose every time an opposition MP left the chamber. He showed his disdain for parliamentary process then, as he is showing it now, by ramming through tax legislation that will vitally affect every citizen and business firm in the country.
(Mr. Rynard.]
Even government spokesmen admit they do not understand all the ramifications of the bill. They even admit that the bill probably contains errors and mistakes. They are still making amendments to it. But Mr. Benson is so determined to get the measure on the statute books before the end of the year that the rights of both Parliament and ordinary citizens are being ridden over roughshod-
In any event, what is now unfolding in Ottawa is systematic contempt for Parliament.
While we are talking about the use of power, I would remind hon. members that Senator Gratton O'Leary spoke in the other place about the disturbing growth of the power of the Prime Minister, adding that the Prime Minister of Canada had more power than even the President of the United States whose actions were controlled by a system of checks and balances and who held office for a dated four-year term. Yes, the government of Canada is neither the House of Commons nor the cabinet: it is the million-dollar plus establishment of the Prime Minister and the office of the Privy Council. These are the ones who are gradually usurping the power of Parliament.
Why continue to have a Parliament, except as the heritage for which people have fought and died so that they might enjoy a system of government in which their voices be heard? The voice of the people will rise again to haunt this dictatorial government. The men in power who stride today across the field of politics are like passing shadows in the night-they come, they go. As Edmund Burke said in the British House of Commons on February 7, 1771: "The greater the power, the more dangerous the abuse." And as Lord Acton said in his "Essays on Freedom and Power": "All power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely." We are seeing an example here today. I repeat, let us hope the voice of the people will be heard again after the next election and that once again the freedom of the people will be restored to Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have a few minutes to express my views on the bill before the House, a bill of the utmost importance. We have reached the end of our many discussions on the bill, and in view of my status I feel I should explain the stand I must take on it.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to note the discussions we have held on the importance of this bill. It all began with a white paper. I thought such action was wise at the time, and I still think it was timely. That statement of policy allowed the people to analyse the importance of the bill. Obviously, since the white paper was published, several needed changes have been made to the proposed tax policy. I should like to point out especially the contribution of the opposition parties and the government to the changes made, if we go back to the early stages of the bill, that is to say the white paper.
I take the liberty of congratulating the opposition parties. They have often raised some valid points. I especially want to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who made a tour of the country to sensitize the people. It was a brilliant idea and the trip of the Leader of the Opposition had some good consequences, since several organizations and provincial governments made after-
December 17, 1971

wards representations to the federal government which realized the importance of some proposed changes. It has therefore decided, as a result of valid points which had been raised, to propose some one hundred amendments.
We would surely be tempted to charge the government with taking a backward step because it has proposed those amendments. I would like, in all objectivity, to congratulate the government for having realized that it was necessary to make the changes proposed by the opposition parties as well as by responsible organizations in the interests of Canadians.
I would like also to recognize the fact that the minister and the government have shown a certain open-mindedness when they accepted the amendments aimed at improving the bill. It is obvious, of course, that this bill is not perfect. We must, however, in all objectivity, recognize the merits of several sections of this bill, as well as the advantages that it contains.
It can still be improved. The minister has even admitted to the House that in the light of experience, he expected to bring forward some amendments, and I hope that he will stick by his intention to make the required changes.
I would also like to express my appreciation concerning the discussions which dealt with the co-operative movement and the caisses populaires. The necessary amendments have been introduced and passed.
I am happy about the representations made in favour of such institutions by many hon. members and many organizations. I am especially happy to see that the government has felt the need to restore to the co-operative movement the particular character that it is necessary for it to have in order to attain its objectives.
I would have hoped that the basic exemptions would be much more than $1,500 and $2,850. In present circumstances, that is obviously insufficient. There is a fairly important improvement, but, as no change had been made in this area in the past 20 years, I feel that the basic exemptions are not high enough, and I hope that the government will seriously consider raising them further in the fairly near future, a move that would be completely justified, especially in the case of certain classes of wage-earners.
I would have hoped also that serious consideration would be given to a special tax allowing for the establishment of an old age security program for people 60 and over. I know that this would require large amounts of money, but as the government has the responsibility to create a proper social climate, it should not hesitate, I think, to develop a tax policy taking into account the establishment of a special tax so that pensioners 60 and over could enjoy a sufficient income. This, in my opinion, would surely constitute another step toward a more just society.
I do hope that within the next few months the government will seriously look into this matter.
I would also like to refer to the speech made last night by the hon. member for Duvernay (Mr. Kierans). I would have hoped, of course, that the government would give much more consideration to the comments of the hon. member for Duvernay. I think this is the best speech I have ever heard in the House regarding tax reform.
Income Tax Act
I believe the hon. member for Duvernay got to the sore spots of our economy and offered advice to which the government should give notice. His words should be considered not only by hon. members but also by the government.
I would like to comment a particular paragraph of his speech that reads as follows:
-a nation's natural resources are not past-production; they are the wealth of its soil and waterways. As such, they cannot be viewed in the same light as current production, as goods and services that we produce each year. Those goods can legitimately be disposed of at will by the people who produce them currently in any given year. Resources are a trust. They have been received from the past. They are to be husbanded by the present generation and they are to be passed on to future generations. A generation that deliberately squanders a nation's natural wealth-I emphasize "deliberately squanders"-to enhance its own standard of living will have much to answer for.
I wish the government would carefully study the hon. member's speech , a speech that could be of direct interest to Canadians. I continue the quotation:
Ten years ago a group of men were named to draft for Canada a fair and just taxation policy that would emphasize growth, employment and stability in the economy. I do not think the task is over. All I want to do is remind the Canadian people and the Canadian government .. . that after ten years that task it not over. This task has to be begun again. I sincerely believe this government can put together all of the elements of an economic policy that will give us growth and employment. In any event, I certainly hope so.
At any rate, it is obvious that the government respects the views of the hon. member for Duvernay and I believe his speech certainly deserves consideration by the government.
In conclusion, I should like to add that there has been much complaint about the motion of closure. I am among those who believe in limiting debates but I feel it is wrong to wait until third reading to limit the debates. It is difficult for parties to come to an agreement in the heat of debate.
Mr. Speaker, the present system may not compell us to commit blunders, but it permits them to exist. I trust we shall apply corrective measures to it, that will enable us to plan a legislative program before each session, so that all hon. members may be aware of the time allowed for debates.
During the forty days given to the consideration of the bill in committee of the whole, hon. members could have been more practical in the discussions. We would have progressed more than we did during the consideration of the bill in committee of the whole, since we were expecting the time of debate to be unlimited.
The government must do some planning; Parliament must plan its business. I believe in limiting debates, provided the limit is established at the beginning of each session, so that we may know how much time we will be allowed to discuss such or such a bill.
Such planning is necessary and once those changes are made we will not have to discuss the implementation of the closure rule which, in certain circumstances, may be fair.
I regret that, at the third reading stage, the debate lasted only four days. In view of the importance of this bill it is obvious that third reading required more time and I think

Mr. Speaker, I will	vote for the bill even though it is
causing deep concern to the public at large. If I refer to the speech of the member for Duvernay, such concern is well known. However, the bill will have beneficial effects for a category of Canadians. I wish to say I am in favor of this tax reform. Even though it is not perfect it is providing some profitable changes for Canadians.

The House resumed, from Friday, November 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Rowland:

That, in the opinion of this House, there should be further improvements made in the operation of the committee system in order to enhance the influence of the House of Commons upon the policy-making process and in order to reduce the information gap between private members and cabinet ministers and to that end that the following subject-matters be referred to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization for the purpose of study apd the making of recommendations (a) the possibility of establishing a means whereby committees could take the initiative in recommending to the House matters which should be referred to them by the House; (b) adequate staff support for committees; (c) the advisability of making it mandatory for each committee to prepare at the end of each session a running record of recommendations it has made to the government and government action taken on its recommendations; (d) making it mandatory for a motion of concurrence to be moved in connection with all committee reports and discovering a means by which debate on such motions could be kept to a reasonable level, specifically the possibility of increasing the number of assigned days, the increase in number to be allocated to the discussion of committee reports, the reports to be considered to be determined by opposition parties; (e) making it possible for minority reports to be tabled together with majority reports from committees; (f) allowing standing committees to be constituted as committees of inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to say that I was here when the motion was first presented by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland). I completely agree with the motion to have the whole committee system reviewed. I want to take only a few minutes to present one or two points because I feel the motion should be brought to a conclusion before five o'clock.
The hon. member for Selkirk came to this House after 1968 and I suspect he has suffered some of the frustations of hon. members like myself and others who came in at that time. We have been active in committees since 1968. In the first year I remember the fisheries committee, for example, sitting for weeks on end discussing various pieces of legislation and the estimates. The members were desirous of clarifying the legislation and having people come before the committee to present their points of view. It has been a frustrating experience because over the last couple of years members have found that the committee system is being treated as an appendage to the House of Commons, with matters being dominated by the party in power to the extent that it becomes a useless exercise.
In the regional economic affairs committee and the fisheries committee we have often worked for weeks on a piece of legislation, only to find out that members who were in no way involved came before the committee and were used as a task force or a special force to get the legislation through without amendment. We found, no matter how much work we had done in connection with amendments and how much research had gone into them, the government was unwilling to accept any changes of substance.
I remember the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Jerome) presenting the point of view here that because under our parliamentary system it is necessary for the House to have confidence in the government, and because the will of the government is expressed in the committees, the committees have become an echo of the House of Commons and it is necessary for that confidence to be extended to committees. I challenge

that. Like the hon. member for Selkirk, I am concerned about the role of our committees.
One of the major difficulties stems from the fact, I suggest to Your Honour, that almost every day members of the House request unanimous consent for certain subject matters to be referred to standing committees. Since coming here I can remember only one occasion when the House accepted a motion under Standing Order 43 and allowed a matter to be referred to a particular committee. There have been numerous occasions, occurring almost daily, when the House has felt it necessary to have a committee investigate a particular circumstance. The most recent example that comes to mind involves the fisheries committee and the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. That example arose because the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), as a result of a tremendous lack of sensitivity regarding the marine resources of Canada-a lack of knowledge, a lack of understanding, a lack of interest and a lack of political backbone necessary to bring into play the decision-making capability that is necessary to enforce obvious rules to conserve the resources of the continental shelf-went his own, unique, unconcerned way and negotiated a series of treaties with European countries. The treaty with Norway is the most recent of such treaties. We have tried to negotiate a treaty with Denmark. We have tried to negotiate one with Portugal and one with Spain. We have one with France and one with the U.K.
There have been motions and arguments by members from the Atlantic region, especially from the province of Newfoundland, suggesting that the whole business ought to be referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. We feel that it is necessary for those committees to consider these questions because the few minutes available when the estimates are considered in the spring will not be enough. These opportunities have been denied us and, since the government has refused to accept legitimate motions calling for the reference of important subject matters to standing committees, I feel that the committee system is being seriously undermined.
We feel, also, that there might be changes in the question period. We wonder whether Canada has the right to go ahead and, without consulting the Atlantic provinces, to negotiate these kinds of treaties in a vacuum. We wonder whether the government has the constitutional or the moral right to make on behalf of Canada this kind of in-vacuum decision. We question whether it is in order for the government of Canada to make these kinds of decisions without referring them to the House of Commons, to the representatives of the Canadian people.
We have felt seriously that the consideration of such treaties would provide a prime opportunity for the various committees involved, the committee on external affairs and the committee on fisheries, to call before them representatives of the Save our Fisheries Association, commonly referred to as SOFA, to call before them representatives of our party coming from the Atlantic region, to summon representatives of the provincial authorities that are so vitally affected and to have the whole matter brought, by means of our committee system,
Improvements to Committees System
before the Canadian people and before the members of the House of Commons.
We are worried about the lack of concern which does not allow such committee representation, because even if that process did not result in any firm resolution or firm decision on the part of the committee, at least it would provide the vehicle necessary for airing the grievances and concerns of frustrated people in the Atlantic region who have not been receiving a legitimate response from the government on this most vital issue that affects their whole future. That is one matter I wanted to put before this House.
I hope that some of the changes suggested by my colleague for Selkirk will be seriously considered and accepted. I recently heard the government House leader make a statement to the effect that it is contemplated there will be changes with respect to the committee system. I do not feel that there is any need for major changes in the rules in this regard if we accommodate some of the legitimate requests that arise from day to day for numerous issues to be referred to our committees.
Last year, in the fisheries committee, I recall we were discussing a particular piece of legislation, the end result being that the issue of conservation, when it came before that committee, could be discussed for only one day. The committee could afford to spend only one day of its time on the matter of fish conservation, principally because the estimates had to be put through by the next day. We had one day to discuss an issue which is one of the most important issues affecting the Atlantic region. When we were able to bring one of our spokesmen from the Atlantic provinces, Mr. Etchegary, President of the Save our Fisheries Association, before that committee to testify, even though he appeared only for a few hours I think the minister and some of his officials were shocked to hear the presentation of facts regarding the tragedy of Atlantic marine resources. We were hurried in that committee and discussed the estimates most inadequately. Actually, the Canadian people would be shocked with our whole parliamentary system if they knew how the committee handled estimates involving several hundred million dollars.
I feel that even within the present rules, Standing Order 43 ought to be utilized more effectively so that we could refer some of these matters to committee. Unless we do that, or unless we amend our procedures regarding the 40-minute question period so that these matters can be delved into in greater detail in the House and bring forward more legitimate responses from the government that is responsible for its behaviour during the question period to the Canadian people, I forecast that in the coming year, 1972, the House of Commons will hardly be a fit place to be in during the question period.
I have been watching, during the last couple of weeks, what has been going on. Speaking as a member who participates actively in the question period, I have watched closely the absolute frustration and demoralization of certain members on this side of the House which has stemmed from their inability to take part actively in the House of Commons proceedings during the question period. We have been getting responses from the government that have frequently misled the House.

Hear, hear!

The government has been frequently misinforming the House and not informing the House. They are not opening up, so to speak, and giving us legitimate responses. Consider the inability of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to answer questions regarding our resource problems. His answers have given rise to much frustration. Unless some way can be found either to enlarge the scope of the question period and provide more legitimate responses from the government, or for more motions under Standing Order 43 to be accepted-many of these motions being on issues that ought to be referred to standing committees-I suggest that the last session of the twenty-eighth Parliament will be one involving great challenges for the Chair and other hon. members.
There is no way that we, the members from the Atlantic region, Mr. Speaker, will take a back seat on the issue of fish conservation and marine resource management. In view of our motions calling for reference of specific subject matters to certain committees, we feel that the government has a responsibility for tabling the documents relating to the treaties and other arrangements entered into with European countries. Under the terms of confederation I do not feel that the government of this country has the right, in a vacuum, to negotiate treaties that are so disadvantageous to the people of the Atlantic region.
That is my small contribution on the matter brought forward by my colleague for Selkirk. I congratulate him for presenting this marvellous motion. It was well researched and it deserves the support of all members of the House.

Mr. Speaker,
I was expecting some other notice of motion to be brought forward today. If you will excuse my unpreparedness, I should like to comment on this notice of motion in the name of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) which was discussed last month. Unfortunately, at that time I was not able to be present in the House. Many hon. members, of course, wish to speak on this matter. If you will forgive my relatively unprepared presentation today,
I should appreciate saying a few words on it.
First, I should like to suggest to the hon. member for Selkirk that it would have been better if the notice of motion had not included in its wording almost everything that it is possible to suggest about our committees. It runs to many parts and contains just about everything but the kitchen sink. This is a complex question and I think there might be some difficulty voting on a motion which attempts to deal with all the frustrations the hon. member might harbour with regard to the committee system. He has included them all in one notice of motion.
I suggest that the motion could have been a little tighter. Even though it is not as tight as it might be, there is no doubt that following the revision of our rules the committee system of the House of Commons is now better than it was. However, I feel there are many areas where it could be improved. I would briefly like to note some of these along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk.
It should be borne in mind that many of my criticisms of the committee system are basically a criticism of Mem-

bers of Parliament, essentially backbenchers, for not making use of the committee system as it now exists. There is great potential in the committee system which is not being used. I feel most strongly that if members of committees, mostly backbenchers with the odd parliamentary secretary who comes along to protect the minister, would attempt to use the committee system more intelligently, we could do a great deal more without any substantial change. An example given immediately prior to my intervention was the fisheries committee.
Much more could be done in the fisheries committee by the backbenchers. I exclude in this case the two parliamentary secretaries who always come prepared. Both are in the chamber, so I obviously have to exempt them. Backbenchers should be willing to do the preparatory work. They could write letters to members of the civil service who are going to appear before a committee and say that such and such a subject will be discussed, will they kindly arrange to have the people who know something about it there. They could write to the minister and say that such and such an area is of concern and would he be prepared to answer the following questions. In this way, the committee system would work a great deal better.
At present, members come to committees relatively unprepared. They hear a brief presentation by the minister or deputy minister and the officials who happen to be there. For the first time their mind is seized of the problem of the particular department. On the spur of the moment, they think that is interesting or may effect the boys back home. They feel they had better ask a question about a particular fish, fishery, boat, subsidy or whatever it may be.
I feel the committee system would work immeasurably better if Members of Parliament would take the trouble to prepare themselves for the meeting. The cry will understandably go up that they do not have time. I have made this complaint myself. Somehow or other there are too many things for Members of Parliament to do. They have to attend the House, the committees, visit their constituencies and, therefore, they feel it necessary to have a committee staff to help them in the real areas of concern. I do not deny that this argument has validity.
I notice that under paragraph (b) of his multisubdivided resolution, the hon. member refers to adequate staff. This is only an aim he is talking about. It is true that staff might be helpful. With the research assistants provided to the opposition and the government, too often the tendency is for members to pick up a piece of paper which some research assistant has prepared, read the question and get a reply from the minister which has been similarly prepared in a sort of limbo government department. There are men there who think up questions and answers. You have an exchange of views between two people, but this is not a meeting of minds. I see a member nodding in agreement. A member asks a question about a subject he knows very little about, through no fault of his own.
Researchers ask questions and researchers answer questions.

The hon. member has said that often the researchers ask the questions and the researchers answer the questions. He has phrased it better than I. A research-
December 17, 1971

er, through the mouth of a member of the opposition, asks a minister a question and a researcher, through the mouth of a minister, replies. If there is a supplementary question, you are into a never-never land of lack of communication because neither really knows what their researcher is talking about. These words are simply being mouthed on both sides of the House. I appreciate the hon. member's assistance in making this point.
If we had committee research staff, the committees might operate in the same way. When an expert witness appears, a committee member may have a researcher sitting beside him and feeding him little notes. The researcher will tell him the thing to do is hit the witness on this subject. While the member is asking a question, the researcher writes out another question and slips it to the member. Once more the member is simply a mouthpiece for the researcher. This is not the most desirable situation. There is some balance between the two, some area where you can use a researcher to get assistance. I hope all hon. members will accept the blame. I place this blame on my own head as well as on the heads of other members. At present we do not do enough work for the committee system. We could do a great deal more. If we did more, we would not be so enthusiastic about getting extra staff.
I know that the time is short, but I would like to touch on one other aspect. With a functioning committee system, the committee is a small group which in my experience is generally very friendly. Even the member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), who sometimes differs with me on the fisheries committee, will agree that we are a friendly, small group. That type of group tends to get seized with the subject of a committee and works out a program for the government or suggests an amendment to the bill. You then get into a very interesting constitutional area. It is the government which will take responsibility for it.
I would be the last to suggest that because the hon. member for Selkirk or the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) participated in a committee and made useful suggestions which the government accepted, and which later turned out to be not quite as good as we thought, that they should be stopped from criticizing us on the ground that they participated in formulating government policy through the committee system. This may sound a trifle esoteric to people in the gallery who are not parliamentarians. However, it is true that we function in this House in a somewhat partisan sense from time to time. I think this was demonstrated in the last hour. I think it is unfortunate if the suggestion is put forward that somehow or other committees can overcome this fact. I do not think it can be overcome. I do not think that under the British parliamentary system it should be overcome. I only make these comments more or less as a warning.
Even though theoretically the academic will quite often tell us that we should have committees which take the best ideas of the New Democratic Party, the Creditiste party, the member for St. John's East and members on this side of the House, and synchronize them in order to come up with the best thinking of the House, where would that leave the adversary system with the responsibility of questioning ministers? I do not know. I do not try to come down one way or another. All I do is raise it as a problem.
Improvements to Committees System
When the academics, who very often do not have any knowledge of this House, suggest how we should rearrange our affairs, they should bear in mind that this is a very realistic problem. I know the hon. member for Selkirk is aware of it. I do not say this as any real criticism of his motion but only to point out that it is something that cannot be overlooked.
The government takes responsibility for legislation. If the taxation proposals on which we just voted turn out to be bad, I do not think the members of the New Democratic Party who voted in the House of Commons committee on the white paper should in any way feel they must not criticize the government. Perhaps at one stage or another in the system of committees, they went along with such and such a proposal. I do not think it would be right for them to feel this way. I hope that people on the outside realize this.
There is another point I would like to mention. Basically, the motion by the hon. member for Selkirk refers to the possibility of establishing a means whereby committees could independently initiate investigations. I am the chairman of the only committee of the House of Commons which has a general reference. It is an accident of history. If anyone has forgotten it, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni knows a great deal about it. An accident led to the establishment of this committee. Its responsibility is to inquire into the problems of pollution in Canada and the plans of the federal government in relation thereto.
It is the only committee having a general reference. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the other members of the steering committee, or the committee itself might well, with me, decide to look into the question of pulp mill pollution, pollution from gold mines, or mercury pollution. Then, of course, we are faced with the enormity of the subject, the number of matters which could be taken up. So if there are to be more committees having general terms of reference, a great deal more in the way of responsibility must be shown by committee members themselves.
Many times, instead of saying, "That nasty minister will not allow me to put in a motion to refer a certain subject to a parliamentary committee," or, "That miserable man, the parliamentary secretary or the leader of the House will not allow me to do so," members will have to say from time to time, "My local problem is important but there are even more important problems to be considered elsewhere in the country."
I know that as chairman of a committee having a general reference I am subject to certain pressures to do one thing or another thing. For example, I received a letter some time ago accusing myself, or members of the committee generally, of being paid off by the pulp and paper industry because we declined to look into pollution from a certain pulp mill in an area where the writer of the letter has his summer home. I am not worried that he accuses me and other members of the committee in this way; we politicians are used to the kicking we get. But if committees became independent, every member would have to bear a great deal more responsibility for what is done. Time is limited, and the committees themselves would
10596

December 17, 1971
Improvements to Committees System
have to come up with solutions which would from time to time go against the grain of an individual regardless of party.
Perhaps I have spoken too negatively on the hon. member's motion. I have no wish to do this, except to the extent of indicating that there are enormous difficulties associated with the committee system and that these difficulties cannot be resolved quickly. Glancing at the motion itself, I find I completely agree that committees should have more initiative in choosing subject matters for consideration instead of the minister telling them what to do on every occasion.
As to the recommendation that there should be adequate staff support, I agree, subject to the observation that though additional staff might well result in committees doing more work, it would not give them any more time in which to do it. Recommendation (c) has in mind making it mandatory for each committee to prepare at the end of each session a running record of the recommendations it has made to the government and of government action taken on those recommendations. I think this is a good proposal. There is no objection to that.
I am not decided about the suggestion that it should be mandatory for a motion of concurrence to be moved in connection with all committee reports, although I remember having myself brought a motion for concurrence before the House without great success. I think the hon. member's comments on minority reports are excellent and I agree with him that useful inquiries might well spring from the findings of standing committees.
Perhaps I might conclude by saying this. With the exception of those held by the present and former parliamentary secretaries to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) and the other parliamentary secretaries who are here this afternoon, most of these jobs are not particularly onerous. If the committees are to be restructured and are to be given more staff, we should encourage the House and the country to regard committee chairmen as being of importance. I feel that a committee chairman should be just as important as a parliamentary secretary.
Hear, hear!

I notice there are some who are kind enough to indicate their approval. It is important that more responsibility be placed on a committee chairman. If he brings in a report at the end of the year saying, "we held no meetings because we could not figure out what to do," someone should be able to ask, "What did you do for your extra pay? You are being paid extra for a special job; for God's sake get off your backside and do it."
The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) says committee chairmen are not paid extra. That is true. My suggestion is that instead of paying parliamentary secretaries extra, the money should be paid to committee chairmen.

speechtext: We'll send you a cheque tomorrow.
Before I get into deeper trouble on this issue, perhaps I should resume my seat.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland)

on having brought this motion forward, particularly at a time when we are nearing the end of the session and possibly the end of a Parliament. This is a good occasion on which to assess what is happening in our committees.
I have been very interested in observing the changes which have been made in the committee system in the last few years and in reaching some conclusions as to the results of those changes. One thing has been most evident. Committees have become very tiring, very difficult and very time-consuming places into which to put a large number of people.
As to the advantages, I really do not see much change at all. There has been one improvement, though, to the extent that the provision for changes in personnel means that an hon. member can take part in the discussion of a specific subject in which he is interested without needing to be involved for a long period of time in the whole field under consideration. For example, should a member be interested in a particular problem which affects his own area, he has an opportunity to become well informed about the circumstances and take part in discussions concerning it without this involvement becoming an annual operation.
What really bothers me about the operations of committees is the way in which the government pursues the idea that it must always maintain its majority. Take, as an example, the agricultural committee, a committee which has had some very heavy legislation before it and which has travelled around the country hearing representations. I am sure there is not a single committee which has experienced a greater turnover in terms of membership. One cannot help noting that whenever a decision is to be made, the government whip ensures that bodies attend the committee meeting in order to participate in the voting.
It is very easy to make the switch that is necessary before a vote is taken. These people vote on subjects they know absolutely nothing about. Indeed, they do not care what the voting is about. They vote the way the minister or his deputy at the meeting wishes them to vote. To be fair about it, the other parties act in the same way, only to a lesser degree. I am sure there are members of the opposition who would be much more in favour of supporting changes in legislation than leaving things the way they were. Obviously, the government takes the position that things should remain as they are.
The previous speaker said a lot of the legislation referred to committees is civil service legislation and a large number of experts have to deal with collective problems which the minister, the deputy minister and others from the department who appear before the committee are not competent to discuss. If the officials are not competent to discuss such a matter, then all you can do is call for the vote and pass it in that way, because if it is discussed members might be convinced-perhaps wrongly-that the legislation should be changed.
I am sure this is true of the income tax bill. No matter what committee the bill had been sent to, the same decision would have been arrived at as the committee of the whole arrived at, which was to pass the bill in its totality. It would not have been cut up because it would never
December 17, 1971

have been put together again. How would we know which provisions affected one department or another, or one particular taxpayer or another? One consideration of the government has always been as to whether we are changing the balance of ways and means.
If I may go back to the subject of the agricultural committee, that committee considered a number of fairly complex bills. For example, it discussed the labelling of poisons legislation and a number of other matters that affected not so much agriculture but allied fields. I think it is safe to say that the committee did make the decisions and they were made fairly quickly. The members of the committee knew something about the subject and sometimes knew more than the officials. The amendments proposed by the committee were not questioned by the officials and as a result were incorporated into the legislation and the legislation became law.
Where the committee witnesses are not competent in their own field, the committee system cannot honestly and effectively make changes to legislation. One area where in my opinion we have slipped backwards is in the sending of estimates to standing committees. Estimates are sent to the various committees for examination, but the system does not work because seldom is there anyone in the committee who is prepared to take responsibility for the theory behind the estimates. As a result, the chairman of the committee says it is a matter of policy and that since the minister is not there the committee cannot discuss it. If there is a technical discussion on a particular item and the official is not there, the chairman usually says that a written answer will be provided at a later date. I suggest the committee system does not work the way we thought it would.
Previously the minister had to come to the House with his estimates and they were before the House until everyone was satisfied that his estimates were acceptable, that they went far enough or that they did not go too far. If a member asked the minister a question on a specific estimate, he got an answer. The minister was allowed to have two officials sitting at a table. If they were unable to supply the answer, he called for another official from the gallery. This was why part of the gallery was reserved for departmental officials.
This is not the case any more. The minister does not have to take responsibility in committee. Some ministers attend the committees regularly, others do not. Some send their parliamentary secretaries, others do not. Some departments send a large number of officials. I am sure the members of the veterans affairs committee would agree with me that every official who could add or subtract anything from the committee's deliberations participated fully in the discussions.
Depending on the chairman of the committee, there are many ways in which officials can speak. On the other hand, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) came to the agricultural committee and told the
Improvements to Committees System
committee that it had to damned well pass the bill and that it would sit until it did. We all know what happened. The country made the decision on that particular minister and piece of legislation. I am sure all members of that committee realize that the legislation itself was not all wrong. There were many good things about it, though sections of it were very bad. Surely if the committee system were functioning properly, the members of the committee would have been able to correct the bad things and strengthen the good things, in which case it would have been acceptable to the committee and to the country, and to hell with the minister. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I bring to Your Honour's attention the fact that there have been certain consultations among the parties. It is generally felt that since this motion did not get the full hour planned when it was stood over from November 19, it might retain its place for another occasion. I think you will find that there is general agreement to this.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that is substantially correct. Since I should like to make a submission to the House on this subject, if it meets with the approval of the House I would move the adjournment of the debate.

On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say, as I said the last time this order was before the House, that I consider this one of the most important topics in terms of parliamentary procedure that we parliamentarians during this finest hour in the week between four and five o'clock on a Friday afternoon have a chance to discuss. I support any assistance Your Honour can give to the House to seek unanimous consent for the motion to retain its position on the order paper.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Perhaps it should be put into position No. 1.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair has one doubt about this. Do I understand that the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) used the terminology that he wished to adjourn the debate? I could not accept that motion because the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) has the floor. I take it that the hon. member for St. John's East is indicating his agreement with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker) that this motion retain its place on the order paper. Agreed.
